props.title: La Dolce Vita
props.initialSlug: Fellini's exploration of Roman high society

sections.content: Federico Fellini's La Dolce Vita (1960) revolutionized cinema with its episodic exploration of Rome's hedonistic high society. Through Marcello Mastroianni's jaded journalist, Fellini crafted a searing critique of celebrity culture and spiritual emptiness that feels eerily prescient today. The film's iconic scenes - Anita Ekberg wading in the Trevi Fountain, the manic paparazzi chasing stories - created a visual language that influenced everything from 8½ (1963) to The Great Beauty (2013). It marked Fellini's transition from neorealism to his more surreal, dreamlike style.

sections.content: The film's influence on depicting modern alienation and excess can't be overstated. Lost in Translation (2003) echoes its themes of disconnection in luxury settings, while The Wolf of Wall Street (2013) draws from its portrayal of spiraling decadence. Fellini's roving camera and episodic structure inspired the New Wave directors, particularly visible in Breathless (1960) and La Notte (1961). The term "paparazzi" itself comes from the character Paparazzo in the film.

The religious imagery throughout La Dolce Vita sets up a stark contrast between traditional values and modern excess. The opening sequence - a helicopter carrying a statue of Christ over Rome - establishes this tension immediately. Similar religious-versus-secular themes appear in later Italian classics like The Conformist (1970) and Cinema Paradiso (1988), though handled with less satirical bite. sections.content: Contemporary filmmakers continue mining La Dolce Vita for inspiration. Sorrentino's work, especially Youth (2015), directly channels Fellini's mix of satire and surrealism. Babylon (2022) borrows its episodic structure and decadent party scenes to critique Hollywood excess. The film's DNA appears in any movie examining celebrity culture through a critical lens, from Mulholland Drive (2001) to Maps to the Stars (2014).
